question: The original arcade Pac-Man was designed to run forever with no ending, yet on level 256 the right half of the maze turns into a jumble of letters and symbols and the game becomes impossible to finish. What goes wrong?
alternative_answers: Integer overflow in the level counter
The level number is stored in one byte, maximum 255
The level counter wraps around to zero
A bug: the fruit-drawing routine draws 256 fruits over the maze
The level variable runs out of bits
Memory corruption from the level counter rolling over
source_excerpt: An integer overflow causes the 256th level to load improperly, rendering it impossible to complete.

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms an integer overflow makes level 256 load improperly and impossible to complete; I found nothing newer that changes this.

explanation: Pac-Man stores the current level number in a single byte, which can only hold values from 0 to 255. When the game reaches level 256, the counter rolls over to zero. The routine that draws the row of fruit symbols at the bottom of the screen uses this value and ends up trying to draw 256 fruits instead of a handful, writing those symbols all over the right half of the maze and wiping out the dots there. With dots missing, the level can never be cleared, which is why players call it the kill screen.

question: Sony's first PlayStation started life as a CD add-on being developed for which rival company's console?
source_excerpt: Nintendo contracted Sony to develop a CD-ROM add-on, tentatively titled the 'Play Station' or 'SNES-CD'.

extra.why_interesting: Sony's console was originally built to help its biggest future rival; Nintendo walked away and created its own competitor.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the PlayStation began as a Nintendo-contracted SNES CD-ROM add-on by Sony, later cancelled.

explanation: The deal for a Super Nintendo CD drive fell apart, so Sony turned the project into a standalone console that then outsold Nintendo.

question: In his 1981 arcade debut in Donkey Kong, what was Mario's profession?
source_excerpt: Because Donkey Kong takes place on a construction site, Mario was made into a carpenter.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows Mario as the world's most famous plumber, but his very first job on a construction site was something else.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Mario article confirms Mario was a carpenter in 1981's Donkey Kong and became a plumber in Mario Bros. (1983); no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: He was known simply as Jumpman and worked as a carpenter on a construction site; the plumbing career only began two years later in Mario Bros.

question: In 2014 Microsoft bought Mojang, the small Swedish studio behind Minecraft. Roughly how many US dollars did it pay?
source_excerpt: Microsoft announced its agreement to purchase Mojang for $2.5 billion on 15 September 2014.

extra.why_interesting: A blocky indie game made by a tiny Swedish studio sold for a sum normally associated with airlines or oil companies.
extra.verification_notes: Microsoft paid $2.5 billion for Mojang per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojang_Studios, so 'Billions' is correct and unaffected by later events.

explanation: The price was about two and a half billion dollars, for a game that had started as one programmer's side project five years earlier.

question: True or false: in The Legend of Zelda games, the green-clad hero you control is named Zelda.
source_excerpt: Link is a character and the protagonist of Nintendo's video game franchise The Legend of Zelda.

extra.why_interesting: The title names the princess, not the hero, and millions of casual players have been calling the wrong character Zelda for decades.
extra.verification_notes: The green-clad protagonist is Link, not Zelda; Zelda is the princess, and playable-Zelda games like Echoes of Wisdom don't change that (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_(The_Legend_of_Zelda)).

explanation: The hero is Link; Zelda is the princess of Hyrule he spends most of the series rescuing or fighting alongside.

question: Atari's table-tennis game Pong, the first arcade hit, was released in which year?
source_excerpt: the first commercially successful video game

extra.why_interesting: Players can anchor on the Atari 2600 of the late seventies or the moon landing of 1969 and reason their way to the right decade.
extra.verification_notes: Pong was released to arcades in North America on November 29, 1972, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pong); no dispute or newer event changes this.

explanation: Pong arrived in 1972, only three years after the moon landing, and the first test machine in a California bar reportedly broke because its coin box was overflowing.

question: What was the name of the last home console Sega ever released before it stopped making hardware?
source_excerpt: the final home video game console manufactured by Sega

extra.why_interesting: Sega was once Nintendo's great rival, and many players never registered that it quietly stopped making consoles altogether.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Dreamcast was Sega's final home console, discontinued in 2001; no newer original Sega home console exists as of 2026 (only retro/mini products and unconfirmed handheld rumors).

explanation: The Dreamcast launched in 1998 but was crushed by the PlayStation 2, and Sega became a games-only publisher in 2001.

question: The Grand Theft Auto series, famous for its American cities, was originally created by a studio in which country?
source_excerpt: The development of Grand Theft Auto began on 4 April 1995 at DMA Design in Dundee.

extra.why_interesting: A series soaked in American car culture and Los Angeles-style cities was actually invented in a small Scottish city.
extra.verification_notes: GTA was created by DMA Design in Dundee, Scotland (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_(video_game)); 'UK' would also be defensible but Scotland is correct and more specific.

explanation: DMA Design in Dundee made the first game in 1997, and the studio later became Rockstar North, still based in Scotland today.

question: The mobile hit Angry Birds was created by a studio from which Nordic country?
source_excerpt: Angry Birds was developed by Rovio Entertainment, a Finnish company.

extra.why_interesting: Players can reason from Finland's reputation for Nokia and mobile phones, and the answer confirms a small country punching far above its weight.
extra.verification_notes: Angry Birds was created by Rovio Entertainment, a Finnish studio; Sega's 2023 acquisition does not change where it was created.

explanation: Rovio from Espoo, near Helsinki, launched the game in 2009, and it became the first mobile game to spawn a Hollywood film.

question: In 2014 excavators dug up thousands of Atari cartridges, including the infamous E.T. game, from a desert landfill in which US state?
source_excerpt: Excavation started on April 26, 2014 as an open event to the public.

extra.why_interesting: A story long dismissed as an urban legend turned out to be real when excavators found the cartridges in the desert.
extra.verification_notes: The Atari cartridges were excavated in 2014 from a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari_video_game_burial

explanation: Atari had dumped its unsold stock near Alamogordo in 1983, and the dig proved a legend many gamers had assumed was a myth.

question: How many ghosts chase Pac-Man around the maze in the original arcade game?
source_excerpt: each of the four ghosts has its own unique artificial intelligence (A.I.), or 'personality'

extra.why_interesting: Everyone can picture the maze, but counting the colourful pursuers takes a moment of real recall.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms four ghosts (Blinky, Pinky, Inky, Clyde) chase Pac-Man in the original arcade game.

explanation: The red, pink, cyan and orange ghosts each have their own hunting style, and only the red one, Blinky, chases you directly.

question: The Witcher games, starring the monster-hunter Geralt, are based on novels by an author from which country?
source_excerpt: It is based on the book series of the same name by Polish writer Andrzej Sapkowski

extra.why_interesting: A fantasy epic that looks Western-medieval on the surface is one of Central Europe's biggest cultural exports.
extra.verification_notes: The games are based on the book series by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Witcher_(video_game_series)).

explanation: Andrzej Sapkowski wrote the books, and the Warsaw studio CD Projekt Red turned them into games that made Geralt a global star.

question: Mickey Mouse, Bugs Bunny and many other classic cartoon characters wear white gloves, even though they are animals. What practical problem did those gloves solve for early animators?
correct_answer: Hands stayed visible against black bodies
alternative_answers: Black hands disappeared against black bodies
To make the hands easier to see
To make hand movements readable on screen
Hands were simpler and faster to draw
To make the characters look more human
headline_answer: Hands stayed visible against black bodies
source_excerpt: black hands couldn't be seen against black bodies in black-and-white films, so white gloves solved this issue.

extra.verification_notes: The widely cited reason is that black hands were invisible against black bodies in black-and-white animation; other reasons (easier drawing, vaudeville tradition) exist but visibility is the standard practical answer (https://collider.com/cartoon-characters-gloves/).

explanation: Early cartoons were drawn in black and white, and characters like Mickey Mouse had solid black bodies with equally black hands. Whenever a hand passed in front of the body it simply disappeared, so gestures were unreadable. Bright white gloves gave the hands contrast and let audiences follow every movement. The gloves also made hands rounder and simpler, which was faster to draw thousands of times, and they made the animal characters feel more human. Walt Disney later said Mickey got gloves so he would not have mouse hands, because he was meant to seem more like a person.

question: In his very first comics in 1938, Superman could not fly. How did he get over tall buildings instead?
source_excerpt: In Action Comics #1, Superman possesses superhuman speed, allowing him to run and leap... but lacks flight.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume flight is Superman's most basic power; the original Superman was a jumper, which the famous 'single bound' line still preserves.
extra.verification_notes: Superman in Action Comics #1 (1938) could not fly and instead leaped over buildings; later flight was added, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The early Superman simply leaped enormous distances, which is why the old slogan says he could leap tall buildings in a single bound. True flight was only added a few years later.

question: The letters 'DC' in the publisher name DC Comics are an abbreviation of which of the company's own comic-book titles?
source_excerpt: DC is an initialism for Detective Comics, a comic book series first published in 1937.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone says 'DC Comics' without noticing the name literally means 'Detective Comics Comics'; the answer feels obvious once heard, especially since Batman fans know Detective Comics #27.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms DC is an initialism for Detective Comics; no name change found (only a 2024 logo refresh).

explanation: Detective Comics was the anthology in which Batman first appeared in 1939, and the title became so identified with the company that its initials became the brand.

question: Wonder Woman's creator, William Moulton Marston, was a psychologist who helped develop which machine, a fitting origin for a heroine with a Lasso of Truth?
source_excerpt: systolic blood pressure test, which became one component of the modern polygraph

extra.why_interesting: Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth suddenly makes sense: her creator spent his scientific career trying to detect lies.
extra.verification_notes: Marston created the systolic blood pressure test that became a component of the modern polygraph (lie detector), so 'helped develop' is accurate; Larson built the device itself.

explanation: Marston devised the blood-pressure test that became a core part of the polygraph, so a magic lasso that forces people to tell the truth was very much on brand.

question: In his 1962 debut issue, the Incredible Hulk was not green. What colour was he?
source_excerpt: After seeing the first published issue, Lee chose to change the skin color to green.

extra.why_interesting: The Hulk is practically defined by being green, so a debut in another colour is a genuine jolt; grey is guessable as a 'monster' colour.
extra.verification_notes: Hulk was grey in Incredible Hulk #1 (1962); Lee changed to green afterward due to colouring inconsistencies.

explanation: Stan Lee wanted a grey monster, but the printers could not keep the shade consistent from page to page, so from the second issue the Hulk turned green and stayed that way.

question: Walt Disney's honorary Oscar for Snow White came with one full-size statuette plus how many miniature ones?
source_excerpt: a special Academy Award consisting of one full-size and seven miniature Oscar statuettes

extra.why_interesting: The player may not know the trophy, but the title of the film hands them the number; the delight is realising the Academy actually did the obvious joke.
extra.verification_notes: Search results from the Walt Disney Family Museum describe the 1938 honorary award as one full-size plus seven miniature Oscar statuettes, matching the claimed answer.

explanation: One tall Oscar for Snow White and seven little ones for the dwarfs, handed over by child star Shirley Temple at the 1939 ceremony.

question: True or false: Simpsons creator Matt Groening named Homer Simpson after his own father.
source_excerpt: Groening named Homer after his father, who himself had been named after the ancient Greek poet.

extra.why_interesting: Homer sounds like a deliberate classical joke, so players suspect a trap; the truth is more personal and more charming.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Groening named Homer after his father, Homer Groening.

explanation: Groening's father really was called Homer, and his mother Margaret and sisters Lisa and Maggie lent their names too. Only Bart was invented.

question: In 1965 France became the third country to launch its own satellite. The satellite was named after which comic-book character?
source_excerpt: France also became the third country after the USSR and US to launch a satellite on its own rocket

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a satellite to carry a stately name; France chose a small, stubborn cartoon Gaul, and the clue 'France' plus 'comic character' leads a thoughtful player straight there.
extra.verification_notes: Astérix was launched 26 Nov 1965 and named after the comic character; France was third country to launch on its own rocket (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astérix_(satellite)).

explanation: The small Gaulish warrior who resists the Roman Empire was a national hero by 1965, and the satellite Astérix is still in orbit today.

question: Tintin walked on the Moon in Hergé's album published in 1954. How many years later did Neil Armstrong do it for real?
source_excerpt: Explorers on the Moon is the seventeenth volume of The Adventures of Tintin, published by Casterman in 1954, created by Hergé.

extra.why_interesting: Players know 1969 but rarely realise how early Tintin got there; working out the gap turns a trivia fact into a small 'aha'.
extra.verification_notes: Explorers on the Moon was published by Casterman as an album in 1954 and Armstrong walked on the Moon in 1969, a gap of 15 years (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorers_on_the_Moon).

explanation: Apollo 11 landed in July 1969, fifteen years after the album Explorers on the Moon, which even got details like weightlessness and a multi-stage rocket broadly right.

question: On the 1969 Apollo 10 mission, the command module was nicknamed Charlie Brown. Which comic-strip character lent his name to the lunar module?
source_excerpt: The command module was given the call sign Charlie Brown and the lunar module the call sign Snoopy. These were taken from the characters in the comic strip, Peanuts.

extra.why_interesting: A NASA mission flying under cartoon names is surprising, but the Charlie Brown clue gives every player a fair path to the beagle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Apollo 10's CM was Charlie Brown and its LM was Snoopy, both from Peanuts; this is a settled historical fact.

explanation: The lunar module Snoopy flew down to within about 15 kilometres of the Moon's surface as a dress rehearsal for Apollo 11, and Snoopy remains NASA's safety mascot to this day.

question: Eiichiro Oda's pirate manga One Piece holds the world record for copies of a single comic series by one author. Roughly how many copies are in circulation?
source_excerpt: over 600 million copies in circulation worldwide

extra.why_interesting: Western players underestimate manga; the true figure puts a single comic series in the same league as the best-selling novels in history.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports over 600 million copies in circulation by March 2026, and says the series holds the Guinness record for most copies of a comic series by a single author (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Piece).

explanation: More than 500 million copies of One Piece have been printed since 1997, which rivals the entire Harry Potter book series.

question: Wolverine did not debut in an X-Men comic. In 1974 he was introduced as a Canadian government agent sent to fight which Marvel giant?
source_excerpt: In his first mission, he is dispatched to stop the destruction caused by a brawl between the Hulk and the Wendigo.

extra.why_interesting: Wolverine is the X-Men's defining character, so fans are surprised he started as a guest villain in someone else's book; the Canadian clue plus 'another hero' narrows it fairly.
extra.verification_notes: Wolverine debuted in Incredible Hulk #180-181 (1974) as a Canadian agent sent against the Hulk; the Wendigo was also in the fight, which is a minor ambiguity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine_(character)).

explanation: Wolverine appeared on the final page of The Incredible Hulk issue 180 and fought both the Hulk and the monster Wendigo in issue 181, a year before he joined the X-Men.

question: The cartoon dog Scooby-Doo was named after a scat phrase Frank Sinatra sings at the end of which of his 1966 hit songs?
alternative_answers: Strangers in the Night by Sinatra
source_excerpt: Silverman came up with the name from the scat syllables in Frank Sinatra's song 'Strangers in the Night'

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a Saturday-morning cartoon dog to be named after a Sinatra ad-lib; players who know the song's scat ending get a satisfying click.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Fred Silverman derived the name Scooby-Doo from Sinatra's scat 'doo-be-doo-be-doo' in 'Strangers in the Night' (1966).

explanation: Sinatra fades out singing 'doo-be-doo-be-doo', and television executive Fred Silverman heard it on a flight and turned it into the name of the Great Dane.

question: Tintin, the Smurfs and the cowboy Lucky Luke were all created by cartoonists from which European country?
source_excerpt: Western comic album series created by Belgian cartoonist, Maurice De Bevere, best known by the pen name Morris, in 1946.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to file Tintin as French, the Smurfs as American because of the cartoon, and Lucky Luke as a Wild West import, when in fact one small country produced all three.
extra.verification_notes: Hergé (Tintin), Peyo (Smurfs) and Morris (Lucky Luke) were all Belgian; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucky_Luke

explanation: Hergé, Peyo and Morris were all Belgian, and Brussels still celebrates its comic-strip heritage with murals and a dedicated museum.

question: A single Claude Monet painting of a hazy sunrise over the harbour at Le Havre ended up giving its name to an entire art movement. Which movement?
source_excerpt: The painting is credited with inspiring the name of the Impressionist movement.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Impressionism as a grand movement; few realise the name was a critic's sneer at one hazy harbour picture.
extra.verification_notes: Impression, Sunrise (Le Havre port at sunrise) is credited with inspiring the name of Impressionism; no conflicting claims or newer developments found.

explanation: The painting was titled Impression, Sunrise, and a critic used the word as an insult in 1874. The painters adopted the jibe, and the name stuck.

question: True or false: Rembrandt's famous painting The Night Watch actually shows a scene taking place in daylight.
source_excerpt: The title is a misnomer; the painting does not depict a nocturnal scene.

extra.why_interesting: The title tells you it's night; the painting itself disagrees.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the painting depicts a daytime scene and the 'Night' title is a misnomer caused by darkened varnish.

explanation: Layers of dirty varnish darkened the canvas so much that people assumed it was a night scene, and the nickname stuck. A cleaning after the Second World War revealed the militia stepping out into daylight.

question: The portrait everyone calls Whistler's Mother, by the American painter James McNeill Whistler, belongs to a national collection in which European capital?
source_excerpt: It is now in the Musée d'Orsay in Paris, having been bought by the French state in 1891.

extra.why_interesting: The quintessential American painting is not in America at all.
extra.verification_notes: Whistler's Mother is owned by the French state and held at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris; the Tate Britain loan (to 27 Sept 2026) is temporary and doesn't change ownership.

explanation: Its real title is Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1, and the French state bought it in 1891. Today it hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.

question: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an broke through into a pit full of life-size clay soldiers, thousands of them. Which emperor's tomb were they guarding?
source_excerpt: a group of farmers... digging a well approximately 1.5 km east of the Qin Emperor's tomb mound

extra.why_interesting: One of the world's great sculptural treasures was found by people looking for water.
extra.verification_notes: Terracotta Army found by well-digging farmers in March 1974 near Xi'an; it guards the tomb of Qin Shi Huang (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army).

explanation: The first emperor of a unified China had the army built to protect him in the afterlife, over two thousand years ago. Each soldier's face is different, and the actual burial mound still has not been opened.

question: Michelangelo signed only one work in his entire career, carving his name onto a strap across the Virgin Mary's chest after overhearing visitors credit the sculpture to someone else. Which sculpture?
source_excerpt: the only piece Michelangelo ever signed.

extra.why_interesting: The most famous sculptor in history was so stung by a misattribution that he broke his own habit, once.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Pietà article confirms it is the only work Michelangelo signed, with the signature on the sash across Mary's chest after he overheard it credited to another sculptor.

explanation: He was in his early twenties when he carved it for St Peter's in Rome. In 1972 a man attacked it with a hammer, and it has stood behind bulletproof glass ever since.

question: The State Hermitage museum in Saint Petersburg keeps a team of several dozen four-legged 'employees' living in its cellars to protect the collection from rodents. What animals?
source_excerpt: live in the museum's basement, and they also appear on the embankment and on the square during summer.

extra.why_interesting: A palace of priceless art relies on an ancient, low-tech security system.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms dozens of cats live in the Hermitage basement to control rodents; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: The tradition goes back to the eighteenth century, when the empress ordered cats brought to the palace to deal with mice. The museum has its own press secretary for them and even holds a yearly cat day.

question: Marcel Duchamp's 1917 piece Fountain, later voted the most influential artwork of the twentieth century by a panel of experts, was a mass-produced object he simply signed and laid on its back. What object?
source_excerpt: a porcelain urinal signed "R. Mutt" ... voted the most influential artwork of the 20th century by 500 British art professionals

extra.why_interesting: The 'most influential artwork of the century' was bought from a plumbing supplier.
extra.verification_notes: Fountain is a porcelain urinal, and the 2004 poll of 500 British art professionals ranked it the most influential artwork of the 20th century; the authorship dispute doesn't change the answer.

explanation: Duchamp signed it with the fake name R. Mutt and submitted it to a New York exhibition, which refused to show it. The original was lost, so the versions in museums today are authorised replicas.

question: Copenhagen's Little Mermaid statue was commissioned by a brewing heir who fell in love with a ballet version of the Andersen tale. Which brewery's fortune paid for her?
source_excerpt: Carl Jacobsen...had been fascinated by a ballet about the fairytale in Copenhagen's Royal Theatre and asked the ballerina, Ellen Price, to model for the statue.

extra.why_interesting: Denmark's gentlest landmark was bankrolled by beer, and the brewery is literally named after the man who paid.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Carl Jacobsen, son of Carlsberg's founder, commissioned the statue after seeing the ballet; no newer events change this.

explanation: Carl Jacobsen's father founded the brewery and named it after his son. The ballerina who inspired the statue refused to pose nude, so the sculptor's own wife modelled the body.

question: Grant Wood's American Gothic shows a stern man with a pitchfork beside a younger woman in front of a farmhouse. The woman was Wood's sister. The man was not a farmer at all, but Wood's... what?
source_excerpt: The male figure was modeled by Dr. Byron McKeeby, the Wood family's dentist from Cedar Rapids, Iowa.

extra.why_interesting: The archetypal American farmer never farmed a day; he filled teeth.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the male model was Dr. Byron McKeeby, Wood's dentist, and the female model was Wood's sister Nan Wood Graham.

explanation: Byron McKeeby looked after the painter's teeth in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, and only agreed to pose on condition that nobody would recognise him. The painting hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

question: The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam was built around one enormous group portrait of a city militia, known as The Night Watch. Which Dutch master painted it?
source_excerpt: prominently displayed in the Rijksmuseum as the best-known painting in its collection.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the title but may not instantly link it to the artist; the payoff is that the famous 'night' scene is not a night scene at all, the darkening came from centuries of grimy varnish.
extra.verification_notes: Rembrandt painted The Night Watch (1642), displayed in the Rijksmuseum as its best-known work, with no attribution dispute or newer development found.

explanation: Rembrandt painted it in 1642, and it was never meant to look nocturnal: the scene is daylight, darkened over centuries by layers of dirty varnish that later cleaning stripped away.

question: The Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre in 1911. The thief, an Italian who had worked at the museum, was finally caught two years later when he tried to sell it to a dealer in which Italian city?
source_excerpt: finally caught when he contacted Alfredo Geri, the owner of an art gallery in Florence, using the name Leonardo V.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a stolen masterpiece is lost to a shadowy black market; in fact the thief simply walked it back to Leonardo's homeland and tried to sell it openly, and the stem's Italian clue gives a reasoning path to the city most tied to Leonardo.
extra.verification_notes: Peruggia was caught in Florence in Dec 1913 after contacting gallery owner Alfredo Geri (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincenzo_Peruggia).

explanation: Vincenzo Peruggia kept the painting in his Paris flat for two years, then carried it to Florence, where the dealer he approached alerted the director of the Uffizi and the police.

question: Which dormant volcano, standing alone above the plains with glaciers close to the equator, is the highest point in Africa?
source_excerpt: the highest mountain in Africa and the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, at 5,895 m (19,341 ft).

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Africa's highest peak as a mountain range summit; it is actually a lone volcano rising straight out of the savanna with glaciers almost on the equator.
extra.verification_notes: Kilimanjaro is a dormant stratovolcano, Africa's highest peak and the highest free-standing mountain, and it still has glaciers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Kilimanjaro).

explanation: At about 5,895 metres, Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is also the tallest free-standing mountain on Earth, rising straight from the plains rather than from a range.

question: Olympus Mons rises about 22 kilometres, nearly two and a half times the height of Everest. On which planet does it stand?
source_excerpt: about 2.5 times the elevation of Mount Everest above sea level

extra.why_interesting: The giant number primes players to think of Earth, then the realisation lands that the tallest known volcano is not on our planet at all.
extra.verification_notes: Olympus Mons is on Mars; its height of about 21.3–21.9 km matches the question's ~22 km and roughly 2.5× Everest's elevation.

explanation: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano so wide and gently sloped that someone standing on its flank could not tell they were on a mountain at all.

question: In April 2010, an ash cloud from a volcano in which country grounded flights across much of Europe for days?
source_excerpt: About 20 countries closed their airspace to commercial jet traffic, affecting approximately 10 million travellers.

extra.why_interesting: Most adults remember the chaos of the grounded flights but may not recall which country's volcano caused it; the unpronounceable name is a fun payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland erupted in April 2010 and its ash closed much of European airspace for days, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The culprit was Eyjafjallajökull, a name so hard to say that newsreaders worldwide simply called it the Icelandic volcano.

question: The Empty Quarter, the largest unbroken sea of sand dunes on Earth, covers the southern part of which peninsula?
source_excerpt: encompassing most of the southern third of the Arabian Peninsula

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Sahara holds every sand record; the biggest continuous sea of dunes is actually on a different continent.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Rub' al Khali covers most of the southern third of the Arabian Peninsula; the 'largest unbroken sea of sand' wording is a common descriptor that I did not verify.

explanation: Known in Arabic as the Rub' al Khali, it spreads across Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates, and much of it was not crossed by Europeans until the 1930s.

question: Which African country takes its name from the desert that runs the full length of its Atlantic coast?
source_excerpt: The country's name derives from the Namib Desert

extra.why_interesting: Countries are usually named after peoples or rivers; this one is named after a desert, and the clue about the Atlantic coast gives a reasoning path.
extra.verification_notes: Namibia is named after the Namib Desert, which spans its whole Atlantic coastline, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia.

explanation: The Namib, often described as the world's oldest desert, meets the ocean in a stretch of fog, shipwrecks and some of the tallest sand dunes anywhere.

question: The giant cactus with upraised arms that appears in nearly every Western film grows wild in only one desert. Which?
source_excerpt: endemic to the Sonoran Desert and is found primarily in western Sonora in Mexico, and in western Arizona in the US

extra.why_interesting: The arm-raising cactus is used as a symbol of every desert in films and cartoons, yet it is native to just one.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia describes the saguaro as endemic to the Sonoran Desert; the few California outliers don't change that (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saguaro).

explanation: The saguaro lives only in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and northwest Mexico, and can take decades to grow its first arm.

question: True or false: deep in the Sahara there are prehistoric rock paintings showing people swimming.
source_excerpt: people with their limbs bent as if they were swimming

extra.why_interesting: Swimming figures painted in the heart of the driest place imaginable sounds like a joke, yet it is real evidence that the Sahara once had lakes.
extra.verification_notes: The Cave of Swimmers in the Gilf Kebir (Sahara, Egypt) has Neolithic paintings of figures that appear to be swimming; interpretation is debated but the claim is widely accepted.

explanation: The Cave of Swimmers in Egypt's Gilf Kebir was painted thousands of years ago, when the Sahara was a land of lakes and grassland, and it later featured in the film The English Patient.

question: Mount Fuji is still classed as an active volcano. In which year did it last erupt?
source_excerpt: The last recorded eruption was the Hōei eruption which started on December 16, 1707...and ended about January 1, 1708.

extra.why_interesting: Fuji looks so serene that people assume it has been quiet for ages or, alternatively, erupted in living memory; the answer is well before modern Japan, but it still buried the shogun's capital in ash.
extra.verification_notes: Fuji's last eruption was the Hōei eruption beginning December 1707, with no eruptions recorded since, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The Hōei eruption of 1707 dropped ash several centimetres deep on Edo, today's Tokyo, and Fuji has been silent ever since.

question: In 1923 an American expedition found the first fossilised dinosaur eggs ever recognised as such, at the Flaming Cliffs in which Asian desert?
source_excerpt: a region of the Gobi Desert in the Ömnögovi Province of Mongolia

extra.why_interesting: Players associate dinosaur discoveries with American badlands; the proof that dinosaurs laid eggs came from a Central Asian desert, found by a man often said to have inspired Indiana Jones.
extra.verification_notes: Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag) lie in the Gobi Desert, Mongolia, where Roy Chapman Andrews's expedition made the first recognised dinosaur egg discovery (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flaming_Cliffs).

explanation: Roy Chapman Andrews's team in Mongolia's Gobi found nests of eggs that proved dinosaurs laid them, and his adventures are often cited as an inspiration for Indiana Jones.

question: The very top of Mount Everest is capped by a sedimentary rock full of fossilised sea creatures. Which rock?
source_excerpt: Peloidal limestone from the summit of Mount Qomolangma contains skeletal fragments of trilobites, ostracods and crinoids

extra.why_interesting: The highest point on Earth is made of ancient sea floor; a player who knows a little geology can reason from 'fossils of sea creatures' to the answer and feel the delight of the paradox.
extra.verification_notes: The summit of Everest is Ordovician marine limestone (Qomolangma Formation) with trilobite, crinoid and ostracod fossils; nothing newer contradicts this.

explanation: Everest's summit is marine limestone laid down on an ocean floor over 400 million years ago and shoved skyward when India collided with Asia, so climbers stand on ancient seabed.

question: The name of the Sahara comes from an Arabic word meaning what?
source_excerpt: The name 'Sahara' is derived from Arabic: صَحَارَى, romanized: ṣaḥārā, a broken plural form of ṣaḥrā'

extra.why_interesting: Players treat 'Sahara' as a proper name with no meaning; realising that 'Sahara Desert' literally says 'Desert Desert' is a small delight they can reason their way to.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives the Sahara's name as from Arabic ṣaḥārā, plural of ṣaḥrāʾ, meaning 'desert'. The literal plural sense ('deserts') is a minor caveat only.

explanation: The Arabic word sahra simply means desert, so 'Sahara Desert' is really saying 'Desert Desert'.

question: When you shine a torch at a cat at night, its eyes seem to glow back at you, yet they never glow in a completely dark room. Why do a cat's eyes shine like this?
correct_answer: A reflective layer behind the retina
alternative_answers: A mirror layer in the eye reflects the light back
Their eyes reflect light to see better at night
Reflective tissue at the back of the eye
Light bounces back off the back of the eye
headline_answer: A reflective layer behind the retina
topic: Pets: dogs, cats and domestic animals
source_excerpt: Lying immediately behind the retina, it is a retroreflector.

extra.verification_notes: Eyeshine comes from the tapetum lucidum, a reflective layer behind the retina that reflects light and doesn't emit it, which matches the claimed answer.

explanation: Cats have a mirror-like layer of tissue behind the retina called the tapetum lucidum. Light that passes through the retina without being absorbed hits this layer and is bounced back through the retina a second time, giving the light-sensing cells a second chance to catch it. That is why cats see so well in dim light. Some of the reflected light escapes back out of the pupil toward the torch, which is the eerie glow you see. Because the eye only reflects light rather than producing it, nothing shines in total darkness. Dogs, deer, cows and many other nocturnal or crepuscular animals have the same layer, while humans do not, which is why human eyes give the dull red-eye effect in flash photos instead.

question: Of the five basic tastes, which one can a cat not detect at all?
source_excerpt: cat Tas1r2 is an unexpressed pseudogene, meaning a functional sweet-taste receptor heteromer cannot form, and thus the cat lacks the receptor likely necessary for detection of sweet stimuli.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all mammals share the same basic tastes; a cat begging for cake is actually after the fat, not the sugar.
extra.verification_notes: Cats' Tas1r2 sweet receptor gene is an unexpressed pseudogene, so they cannot taste sweet (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1183522/); the other four basic tastes are detectable.

explanation: Cats carry a broken version of the sweet-receptor gene, so sugar does nothing for them. A cat licking your ice cream is after the fat.

question: Virtually every pet golden hamster in the world descends from one mother and her litter dug out of a field in 1930 near which Middle Eastern city?
source_excerpt: all domestic golden hamsters are descended from one female – likely the one captured in 1930 in Syria.

extra.why_interesting: A hamster feels like a generic pet-shop animal, yet the entire worldwide population traces back to one hole in the ground in Syria.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1930 hamster mother and litter were found near Aleppo, Syria by Israel Aharoni, and that domestic hamsters trace to that single female.

explanation: That is why the breed is called the Syrian hamster. A zoologist from Jerusalem collected the family, and their descendants filled pet shops across the globe.

question: True or false: Dalmatian puppies are born with their spots already showing.
source_excerpt: Dalmatian puppies are born with plain white coats and their first spots usually appear within 10 days; however, spots may be visible on their skin from birth.

extra.why_interesting: The spots are the breed's whole identity, so players assume a newborn Dalmatian already has them.
extra.verification_notes: Dalmatian puppies are born with plain white coats and spots appear within about 10 days, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalmatian_(dog)).

explanation: Newborn Dalmatians are pure white. The spots start to appear after about two weeks and keep developing for months.

question: Which hunting breed from central Africa is nicknamed the 'barkless dog' because it yodels instead of barking?
source_excerpt: a breed of hunting dog created from stock that originated in Central Africa

extra.why_interesting: Barking is what defines a dog for most people; a breed that physically does not do it is a delightful exception.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Basenji is a Central African hunting breed nicknamed the 'barkless dog' that makes a yodel-like sound.

explanation: The Basenji's unusually shaped larynx produces a yodel rather than a bark. It was prized by hunters in the Congo for exactly that quiet.

question: The oldest cat ever recorded reached roughly what age?
source_excerpt: Creme Puff who was born on 3 August 1967 and lived until 6 August 2005 - an amazing 38 years and 3 days

extra.why_interesting: Players know a cat lives maybe 15 years; the record-holder lasted roughly as long as a human career.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness and Wikipedia record Creme Puff as the oldest cat ever at 38 years 3 days, and no newer verified record exists (oldest living cat Flossie was about 30 in Dec 2025).

explanation: Creme Puff of Austin, Texas lived 38 years, from 1967 to 2005. Her owner credited an odd diet that included bacon, eggs and coffee with cream.

question: A Siamese cat is dark on its face, ears, paws and tail but pale everywhere else. What is true of those dark body parts that explains the pattern?
alternative_answers: They are colder than the body
source_excerpt: The mutated tyrosinase enzyme is heat-sensitive; it fails to work at normal body temperatures but becomes active in cooler (< 33 °C) areas of the skin.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone recognises the Siamese pattern but almost nobody has asked why it is that pattern; the answer turns the cat into a living thermometer.
extra.verification_notes: Siamese colorpoint comes from a heat-sensitive tyrosinase that is active only in cooler skin areas (extremities), per Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siamese_cat.

explanation: The pigment enzyme in Siamese cats only works below body temperature, so colour appears on the chilly extremities. Siamese kittens are born almost white because the womb is warm all over.

question: What breed of dog played Toto in the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz?
source_excerpt: Terry was a female Cairn Terrier who appeared in many different movies, most famously The Wizard of Oz (1939).

extra.why_interesting: Toto is one of the most famous dogs on film, yet most viewers have never put a breed name to the little black dog.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Toto in the 1939 Wizard of Oz was played by Terry, a Cairn Terrier.

explanation: Toto was played by a female Cairn Terrier named Terry, who reportedly earned more per week than some of the human actors playing Munchkins.

question: Larry, a tabby cat who holds the official title Chief Mouser, has lived since 2011 at which famous London address?
source_excerpt: Larry is a domestic tabby cat who has been the Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office at 10 Downing Street since 15 February 2011.

extra.why_interesting: An official government job title for a cat is funny on its own, and the player gets a proud click when the address lands.
extra.verification_notes: Larry has been Chief Mouser at 10 Downing Street since 2011 and is still there as of Sept 2026, serving PM Andy Burnham; the August 2026 death report was retracted (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_(cat)).

explanation: Larry has outlasted several prime ministers at Number 10. He belongs to the building rather than to any politician, so he stays when they move out.

question: The Saint Bernard breed takes its name from a mountain hospice on an Alpine pass that connects which two countries?
source_excerpt: links Switzerland with Aosta in the region Aosta Valley in Italy.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the brandy-barrel rescue dog but rarely connect the name to a real mountain road and the monks who bred them.
extra.verification_notes: The Great St Bernard Pass, home of the hospice the breed is named after, links Switzerland and Italy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_St_Bernard_Pass).

explanation: Monks at the Great St Bernard Pass hospice bred the dogs to find travellers lost in snow. One dog, Barry, is credited with saving around 40 lives.

question: Guinea pigs are neither pigs nor from Guinea. On which continent were they first domesticated?
source_excerpt: first domesticated as early as 5000 BC for food by tribes in the Andean region of South America

extra.why_interesting: The name points to Africa and to pigs; the truth is a rodent from the mountains of Peru.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms domestication began in the Andean region of South America, and that the animals are neither pigs nor from Guinea.

explanation: They were tamed thousands of years ago in the Andes, and in Peru and Bolivia they are still a traditional dish called cuy.

question: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev gave a puppy called Pushinka, the daughter of a dog that had orbited the Earth, to the family of which US president?
source_excerpt: Pushinka was the daughter of Strelka, who had travelled into space aboard Korabl-Sputnik 2.

extra.why_interesting: A Cold War diplomatic gift being a space dog's puppy is pure delight, and the space-race era points a thoughtful player to the right president.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Khrushchev gave Pushinka, daughter of orbiting dog Strelka, to JFK in 1961.

explanation: Pushinka's mother Strelka flew to orbit and back in 1960. The puppy later had pups of her own with the Kennedys' dog, which the president nicknamed 'pupniks'.

question: Snoopy, Charlie Brown's dog in the Peanuts comic strip, belongs to which breed?
source_excerpt: A largely anthropomorphic beagle, Snoopy is nearly the polar opposite of his owner, Charlie Brown.

extra.why_interesting: One of the most drawn dogs in history, instantly recognisable, yet naming the breed takes a small beat of thought.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Snoopy is a beagle owned by Charlie Brown; no newer development changes this.

explanation: Charles Schulz based Snoopy partly on a childhood dog of his own, and the beagle has sat on top of his doghouse since 1950.

question: Most beer is sold in brown or green glass, while wine and spirits are happily sold in clear bottles. Why do brewers avoid clear glass?
alternative_answers: Dark glass blocks sunlight that spoils beer
To prevent lightstruck or skunked flavour
Sunlight ruins the taste of beer
Protects the hops from light damage
topic: Drinks: coffee, tea, wine and beer
source_excerpt: Lightstruck (or sunstruck) flavor in beer produces the so-called skunky flavor, caused by light of both visible and ultraviolet wavelengths affecting the product adversely.

extra.verification_notes: Light reacts with hop iso-α-acids and riboflavin to form MBT (skunky flavor); brown/green glass filters this, clear does not (Difford's Guide).

explanation: Hops contain bitter compounds called iso-alpha acids. When ultraviolet and blue light hit them, they break down and react with sulphur compounds in the beer, producing a chemical almost identical to the one in skunk spray. The result is the harsh 'skunked' or 'lightstruck' flavour of beer left in the sun. Brown glass blocks nearly all of this light, green glass blocks some, and clear glass blocks almost none. Brewers who use clear bottles typically rely on specially modified hop extracts that do not react to light. Wine and spirits contain no hop compounds, so light is far less of a problem for them.

question: Despite its name, the arabica coffee plant is native to which country?
source_excerpt: Endemic to the southwestern highlands of Ethiopia, Coffea arabica is grown in dozens of countries between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Tropic of Cancer.

extra.why_interesting: The name points the player straight at Arabia; the plant actually comes from the Horn of Africa, and the name only records where it was first traded.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives Ethiopia as the native origin of Coffea arabica; the South Sudan (Boma Plateau) wild population is a minor nuance that doesn't create a competing answer.

explanation: Arabica grows wild in the Ethiopian highlands and only got its name because Yemeni traders on the Arabian Peninsula made it famous.

question: Which country drinks the most coffee per person in the world?
source_excerpt: Finland typically occupying the top spot with a per-capita consumption of 12 kg (26 lb) per year, followed by Norway, Iceland, Denmark, The Netherlands, and Sweden.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Italy or Brazil; the answer is a cold Nordic country where coffee breaks are written into labour agreements.
extra.verification_notes: Finland is the standard top per-capita coffee consumer per Wikipedia; Luxembourg's higher figures in some datasets are skewed by commuters, so this is only a minor ambiguity.

explanation: Finns drink roughly 12 kilograms of coffee per person each year, far ahead of Italy, and the Nordic neighbours fill the next spots.

question: True or false: arabica beans, the premium coffee variety, contain more caffeine than the cheaper robusta beans.
source_excerpt: contains more caffeine (2.7% compared to arabica's 1.5%)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the premium, pricier bean must be the stronger one; in fact the cheap, bitter robusta packs about double the caffeine.
extra.verification_notes: Robusta contains roughly double the caffeine of arabica (2.7% vs 1.5%), so the statement is false and the claimed answer 'False' is correct; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robusta_coffee

explanation: False. Robusta has roughly twice the caffeine of arabica, which is one reason it tastes harsher and is favoured for strong espresso blends and instant coffee.

question: Green, black, white and oolong tea are all made from the leaves of how many different plant species?
source_excerpt: Tea is an aromatic beverage prepared by infusion of hot or boiling fresh water with fresh or cured leaves of Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub native to East Asia

extra.why_interesting: The teas look and taste so different that players assume several plants; the answer is one, and only the processing differs.
extra.verification_notes: All true teas (green, black, white, oolong) come from Camellia sinensis, so 'one' is correct, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea.

explanation: They all come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, and the colour and flavour depend only on how much the leaves are allowed to oxidise after picking.

question: Britain and China usually spring to mind, but which country actually drinks the most tea per person?
source_excerpt: Turkey 3.16 kg (6.96 lb)

extra.why_interesting: Britain is the stereotype and China the volume giant, but per head the champion is Turkey, where tea is served in small tulip glasses all day long.
extra.verification_notes: Turkey is ranked first in per-capita tea consumption (3.16 kg) ahead of Ireland and the UK, and the article says it still leads as of 2025; the underlying data is from 2016 and I did not search for newer rankings.

explanation: Turks drink around 3 kilograms of tea per person a year, served black in small tulip-shaped glasses, which puts them well ahead of the British.

question: Archaeologists have found the oldest known evidence of winemaking, around 8,000 years old. In which country?
source_excerpt: The earliest known traces of wine were found near Tbilisi, Georgia (c. 6000 BCE).

extra.why_interesting: Players guess Italy, Greece or Iran; the earliest wine jars come from a small Caucasus country that still ferments wine in buried clay vessels.
extra.verification_notes: Georgia's 8,000-year-old jars (c. 6000 BCE) remain the oldest known evidence of grape winemaking; no newer find overturns this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_wine).

explanation: Residue in Neolithic clay jars from Georgia dates to about 6000 BC, and Georgians still make wine in buried clay vessels called qvevri today.

question: In the late 1800s a tiny insect pest destroyed most of Europe's vineyards. The vines were saved by grafting them onto resistant rootstocks from which continent?
source_excerpt: Leo Laliman and Gaston Bazille, two French wine growers, proposed that the European vines be grafted to the resistant American rootstock.

extra.why_interesting: The pest itself came from America, and the fix came from the same place: almost every famous French vine today grows on American roots.
extra.verification_notes: Phylloxera was overcome by grafting European vines onto resistant North American rootstock; 'most of Europe's vineyards' is loose but the answer is unambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight).

explanation: The pest, phylloxera, had arrived from America, and American vine roots had evolved to resist it, so nearly every great European vine today grows on American roots.

question: The juice of almost every red wine grape is actually colourless. So which part of the grape gives red wine its colour?
source_excerpt: In non-teinturier red grapes, anthocyanin pigments are confined to the outer skin tissue only, and the squeezed grape juice of most dark-skinned grape varieties is clear.

extra.why_interesting: The surprising premise, that the juice is clear, forces the player to reason their way to the skins, which also explains how white wine can be made from red grapes.
extra.verification_notes: Anthocyanins in the skins colour red wine; only rare teinturier grapes have coloured juice, which the question's 'almost every' covers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teinturier_grape).

explanation: The pigment sits in the skins, which stay in the fermenting juice for red wine, and that is why champagne can be made from red grapes if the skins are removed quickly.

question: The world's first pale golden lager was brewed in the Bohemian city of Plzeň. In which year?
source_excerpt: 5 October 1842 First brew of Bavarian type beer, bottom-fermented beer, so-called pale lager.

extra.why_interesting: Golden beer feels ancient, but it is younger than the railway; before the 1840s nearly all beer was dark and cloudy.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Pilsner Urquell Brewery article dates the first pale lager brew in Plzeň to 5 October 1842, and no source disputes it.

explanation: Josef Groll brewed the first clear golden lager in Plzeň in 1842, and within a few decades it had become the style most of the world calls beer.

question: Bavaria's famous 1516 beer purity law allowed only water, barley and hops. Which essential brewing ingredient was left out, because nobody yet knew it existed?
source_excerpt: the only ingredients used for the brewing of beer must be Barley, Hops and Water.

extra.why_interesting: Players know beer has four ingredients and the stem names three, so the gap is reasoned out, and the payoff is that brewers were using it without knowing it existed.
extra.verification_notes: Yeast is the standard answer: the 1516 Reinheitsgebot listed only water, barley and hops, and yeast's role wasn't understood until later (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinheitsgebot).

explanation: Brewers were adding yeast with every batch without realising it, and its role in fermentation was only explained by Louis Pasteur some 350 years later.

question: The hop plant, which gives beer its bitterness, belongs to the same botanical family as which controversial plant?
source_excerpt: Hemp (Cannabis) and hop (Humulus) are the most economically important species

extra.why_interesting: Nobody connects the pub with the dispensary, yet the two plants are close botanical cousins, and the word 'controversial' gives a fair foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Hops (Humulus) and Cannabis are both in Cannabaceae per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabaceae.

explanation: Hops and cannabis are both members of the Cannabaceae family, and their resinous flowers share many of the same aromatic compounds.

question: The pH scale for measuring acidity was invented in 1909 at the research laboratory of which brewery?
source_excerpt: In 1909, the Danish chemist Søren Peter Lauritz Sørensen introduced the concept of pH at the Carlsberg Laboratory

extra.why_interesting: A cornerstone of school chemistry was born in a brewery's research lab, because brewers needed to control acidity to brew consistently.
extra.verification_notes: Sørensen introduced pH in 1909 at the Carlsberg Laboratory (Carlsberg brewery's research lab), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH.

explanation: Danish chemist Søren Sørensen devised the pH scale at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen, where he was studying how acidity affects brewing enzymes.

question: Brazil grows more coffee than any other country. Which Southeast Asian nation comes second?
topic: Drinks: coffee, tea, wine and beer
source_excerpt: Vietnam ranks second, producing 31.7 million 60-kilogram bags, or 18% of global coffee production.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture coffee as a Latin American or Ethiopian crop and reach for Colombia; the answer sends them to Southeast Asia, where the bitter robusta bean in their instant coffee and espresso blends mostly comes from.
extra.verification_notes: Vietnam remains the world's second-largest coffee producer (~31.7M bags in 2025/26, about 18% of world output) behind Brazil, per search summaries of aggregator sites such as https://www.visualcapitalist.com/the-worlds-largest-coffee-producers/.

explanation: Vietnam overtook Colombia in the late 1990s and now grows mostly robusta, the strong, bitter bean that ends up in instant coffee and many espresso blends.

question: In which stage of sleep are your eyes darting about under the lids while almost every other muscle in your body is switched off?
source_excerpt: REM atonia, an almost complete paralysis of the body, is accomplished through the inhibition of motor neurons.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture sleep as the body 'resting', not as the brain actively switching the muscles off; realising the stage named for darting eyes is also the stage of near-total paralysis is a small jolt.
extra.verification_notes: REM sleep is defined by rapid eye movements with near-complete skeletal muscle atonia, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_eye_movement_sleep.

explanation: The brain deliberately paralyses the body during rapid eye movement sleep so you don't physically act out your dreams.

question: True or false: each basic taste, such as sweet or bitter, can only be detected by its own dedicated zone of the tongue.
source_excerpt: every taste sensation can come from all regions of the tongue, though certain parts are more sensitive to certain tastes.

extra.why_interesting: Generations learned the tongue map at school, so most players confidently answer True, and the correction is a genuine 'wait, really?' moment.
extra.verification_notes: The tongue map is a debunked myth; all tastes can be detected across all regions of the tongue (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue_map).

explanation: The famous tongue map is a myth that came from a mistranslated German paper; taste buds across the whole tongue can detect every basic taste.

question: Surgeons sometimes operate on a patient's brain while the patient is awake and chatting. What does brain tissue lack that makes this possible?
source_excerpt: Your brain does not have any pain receptors, so you will not feel any pain during the time the surgeon is operating on it.

extra.why_interesting: The organ that processes every pain you have ever felt cannot feel pain itself; players assume touching the brain would be agony.
extra.verification_notes: Brain tissue has no pain receptors, which is the standard explanation for awake craniotomy; the scalp is numbed locally (https://www.cuh.nhs.uk/patient-information/living-with-a-brain-tumour-undergoing-an-awake-craniotomy/).

explanation: The scalp and skull are numbed, but the brain itself has no pain receptors, so patients can stay awake and help surgeons avoid areas controlling speech or movement.

question: Melatonin, the hormone that tells your body it is night, is made by a tiny pea-sized gland deep in the brain. Which gland?
source_excerpt: It produces melatonin, a serotonin-derived hormone, which modulates sleep patterns following the diurnal cycles.

extra.why_interesting: Most people know melatonin from pharmacy shelves but have no idea the body makes it in a gland that a famous philosopher thought housed the soul.
extra.verification_notes: The pineal gland produces melatonin; the 'pea-sized' wording is loose (Wikipedia says rice-grain size, 5–8 mm) but doesn't affect the answer.

explanation: The pineal gland releases melatonin when it gets dark, and the philosopher Descartes was so struck by it that he called it the seat of the soul.

question: The coiled organ in your inner ear that turns vibrations into nerve signals is named after which animal, because of its shape?
source_excerpt: derived from the Latin word for snail shell, which in turn is from the Ancient Greek κοχλίας kokhlias ("snail, screw")... in reference to its coiled shape.

extra.why_interesting: A player who pictures the inner ear's spiral can reason their way to the animal, and the name is the same Latin-derived word in most European languages.
extra.verification_notes: Cochlea derives from the Latin for snail shell and the Greek kokhlias ('snail'), named for its coiled shape, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlea.

explanation: It's the cochlea, from the Greek word for snail, and it really is a tightly coiled spiral tube about the size of a pea.

question: Every human eye has a small patch that cannot see anything, and your brain simply fills in the gap. What exits the eye at that exact spot?
source_excerpt: the lack of light-detecting photoreceptor cells on the optic disc of the retina where the optic nerve passes through.

extra.why_interesting: Players don't realise they are permanently blind in part of each eye; the reason is a wiring choice the brain quietly papers over every second.
extra.verification_notes: The blind spot is the optic disc where the optic nerve exits the retina, and it is present in all human eyes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_spot_(vision)).

explanation: Where the optic nerve leaves the retina there is no room for light-sensing cells, so each eye has a blind spot that your brain hides by filling it in.

question: Your brain is only about two percent of your body weight. Roughly what share of your body's energy does it use when you are resting?
source_excerpt: The human brain accounts for about 2% of body weight but about 20% of the body's resting energy consumption.

extra.why_interesting: A player can estimate from the brain being a small fraction of body mass, then be surprised that it burns ten times its share.
extra.verification_notes: The brain is about 2% of body mass and uses about 20% of resting energy, per the PNAS paper on brain energy demand (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1816908116); I found no newer findings that contradict it.

explanation: The brain burns around a fifth of your resting energy, about ten times its share by weight, mostly to keep billions of neurons firing.

question: Three of these animals can sleep with one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half awake. Which one cannot?
source_excerpt: The phenomenon has been observed in a number of terrestrial, aquatic and avian species.

extra.why_interesting: The dolphin is the famous half-brain sleeper, so players waste it as a wrong guess; the trick is knowing a duck can do it too, leaving the cat as the only animal that must shut down fully.
extra.verification_notes: Dolphins, mallards and northern fur seals all show unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, while cats sleep bilaterally, so Domestic cat is the only valid answer.

explanation: Dolphins, fur seals and mallard ducks all do half-brain sleep to keep breathing or watching for predators, while a cat sleeps the way we do, with the whole brain off.

question: In 2017 three American scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine for working out the genes behind a roughly 24-hour cycle in living things. What is this cycle called?
source_excerpt: Discoveries of Molecular Mechanisms Controlling the Circadian Rhythm

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the body clock is old, settled science; learning the genes behind it won a Nobel Prize less than a decade ago reframes it as a modern discovery.
extra.verification_notes: The 2017 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine went to Americans Hall, Rosbash and Young for the molecular mechanisms controlling the circadian rhythm; see https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2017/advanced-information/

explanation: Hall, Rosbash and Young uncovered the genes that make cells keep daily time, the internal clock that governs when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert.

question: Some people involuntarily see colours when they hear music or read letters, because one sense triggers another. What is this condition called?
source_excerpt: a perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory or cognitive pathway leads to involuntary experiences in other sensory or cognitive pathways

extra.why_interesting: The description sounds like poetry or a drug trip, yet it is a recognised neurological trait with a single name that interested adults have met in articles about famous musicians.
extra.verification_notes: Synaesthesia (British spelling of synesthesia) is the correct term for one sense involuntarily triggering another, including music-to-colour and letter-to-colour forms; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synesthesia.

explanation: Synaesthesia is a harmless crossing of the senses, and several famous musicians and artists have described seeing their music in colour.

question: The German chemist Kekulé said a daydream of a snake biting its own tail revealed the ring-shaped structure of which compound?
source_excerpt: reverie or day-dream involving a snake seizing its own tail

extra.why_interesting: A snake biting its tail is a circle, and a player who knows a little chemistry can leap from 'circle' to the famous ring molecule, a satisfying deduction rather than pure recall.
extra.verification_notes: Kekulé's own account (1890) described a reverie/day-dream of a snake seizing its tail leading to benzene's ring structure; the question's 'said' wording accommodates doubts about authenticity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Kekulé).

explanation: Kekulé's ring of six carbon atoms, proposed in 1865, became one of the foundations of organic chemistry, and he credited the idea to that dozing vision.

question: In 1964 a 17-year-old Californian student set a famous record by staying awake, without stimulants, for roughly how many days?
source_excerpt: 11 days and 25 minutes (264.4 hours)

extra.why_interesting: Most players guess two or three days because that is the limit of their own experience; the real figure is long enough to feel almost impossible.
extra.verification_notes: Gardner stayed awake about 11 days (264 hours) at age 17 (Dec 1963–Jan 1964); later records don't contradict the 'famous record' wording.

explanation: Randy Gardner went 264 hours without sleep, suffering hallucinations and memory lapses, and Guinness later stopped listing the category as too dangerous.

question: Which part of the human brain, although it takes up only about a tenth of the brain's volume, contains more neurons than all the rest of the brain put together?
source_excerpt: the cerebellum contains more neurons than the total from the rest of the brain, but takes up only 10% of the total brain volume.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the big wrinkled cerebral cortex, home of thought and language, must hold most of the brain's neurons. In fact the small structure at the back that handles balance and coordination packs in more neurons than everything else combined.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Cerebellum article states the cerebellum holds more neurons than the rest of the brain combined while taking up about 10% of brain volume.

explanation: The cerebellum, tucked under the back of the brain, packs in around 69 of the brain's roughly 86 billion neurons, far more than the famous wrinkled cortex. Its tiny, densely packed granule cells are what inflate the count.

question: Liechtenstein flew a plain blue-and-red horizontal bicolour for decades, then in 1937 suddenly added a golden crown to it. What embarrassing discovery the year before prompted the change?
correct_answer: It was identical to Haiti's flag
alternative_answers: It was the same as Haiti's flag
It clashed with Haiti's flag at the 1936 Olympics
Another country used the same flag
It was indistinguishable from another nation's flag
headline_answer: It was identical to Haiti's flag
topic: Flags, anthems, capitals and national symbols
source_excerpt: its flag was identical to the flag of Haiti

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Liechtenstein discovered at the 1936 Olympics that its flag was identical to Haiti's, prompting the 1937 crown.

explanation: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, Liechtenstein's team discovered that their national flag was exactly the same as the civil flag of Haiti, a blue-over-red bicolour on the other side of the Atlantic. To avoid being confused with Haiti at international events, the principality added a golden princely crown to the upper hoist corner in 1937, giving the flag a unique symbol while keeping the historic colours.

question: Every national flag in the world has four corners except one. Which country's flag is made of two stacked triangles?
source_excerpt: It is the only non-rectangular national flag in the world and the only one that is taller than it is wide.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every flag in the world is a rectangle; one Himalayan country breaks the rule entirely, and the shape is strange enough that most people have seen it without registering it.
extra.verification_notes: Nepal is the only non-rectangular national flag and its design is unchanged since 1962; the 'two stacked triangles' phrasing is a standard simplification.

explanation: The two pennants are said to represent the Himalayan peaks, and the sun and moon on them stand for the hope that the nation lasts as long as those heavenly bodies.

question: The Union Jack combines the crosses of three patron saints. Which of the four nations of the United Kingdom is not represented on it at all?
source_excerpt: Wales having been considered an integral part of the Kingdom of England at the time the flag of Great Britain was created in 1606.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes the flag of the United Kingdom represents all its nations, then realises one of the four is missing entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Union Flag has crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick only; Wales has no representation and no official change has occurred (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Jack).

explanation: When the flag was designed, Wales was already treated as part of the Kingdom of England, so it never got its own cross, which is why its red dragon flies separately today.

question: A white band curves across the blue globe on Brazil's flag. What two-word motto is written on it?
source_excerpt: Ordem e Progresso (Order and Progress)

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone can picture the green, yellow and blue flag, but very few have ever read the words written across the middle of it.
extra.verification_notes: The motto on Brazil's flag is 'Ordem e Progresso' (Order and Progress); the proposal to add 'Amor' has not been adopted.

explanation: The motto comes from the positivist philosophy of Auguste Comte, which was fashionable among the officers who overthrew the Brazilian monarchy in 1889.

question: Which country splits its government across three capital cities, one each for the executive, the legislature and the courts?
source_excerpt: Pretoria: Administrative and executive capital; Cape Town: Legislative capital; Bloemfontein: Judicial capital

extra.why_interesting: Players expect every country to have one capital; this one spreads the three branches of government across three different cities.
extra.verification_notes: South Africa is the only country with executive (Pretoria), legislative (Cape Town) and judicial (Bloemfontein) capitals, and no recent change is listed.

explanation: Pretoria houses the government, Cape Town the parliament and Bloemfontein the top courts, a compromise struck when four colonies merged in 1910.

question: Indonesia's flag is a plain red band above a plain white one. Which tiny European state flies an almost identical flag, differing only in its proportions?
source_excerpt: The flag of Monaco is graphically similar to the flag of Indonesia, with differences in their shades of red and dimension ratios.

extra.why_interesting: A tiny Riviera principality and a huge Southeast Asian nation share what is essentially the same flag, and most people have never noticed.
extra.verification_notes: Monaco's flag is graphically near-identical to Indonesia's, differing mainly in ratio (4:5 vs 2:3) and slightly in red shade; no other tiny European state fits.

explanation: Monaco's flag is slightly squarer than Indonesia's, and the principality reportedly objected when Indonesia adopted its design in 1945, but Indonesia pointed out its colours were centuries older.

question: Canada's red-and-white flag with the single maple leaf seems timeless, but it is surprisingly recent. In which year was it first raised?
source_excerpt: The new national flag was inaugurated on February 15, 1965, at an official ceremony held on Parliament Hill in Ottawa

extra.why_interesting: The maple leaf feels ancient and inevitable, yet it is younger than many quiz players; before it Canada flew a flag with the Union Jack in the corner.
extra.verification_notes: The maple leaf flag was first raised on February 15, 1965, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Canada, and the other options are unrelated dates.

explanation: Until 1965 Canada flew the Red Ensign with the Union Jack in the corner, and the switch followed a bitter months-long parliamentary fight known as the Great Flag Debate.

question: The Philippines normally flies its flag with the blue band on top. What does it signal when the flag is officially flown the other way up, red band on top?
alternative_answers: That the country is at war
source_excerpt: To indicate a state of war, the red field is flown upwards and is placed on the right (i.e., the observer's left) when hung vertically.

extra.why_interesting: Flying a flag upside down is normally a mistake or a distress signal; here it is an official, deliberate message with a very specific meaning.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the red field is flown up to indicate a state of war, consistent with RA 8491; no newer developments found.

explanation: The flag is the only national flag whose orientation carries an official meaning, with blue up for peace and red up when the nation is at war.

question: Despite its name, the French anthem La Marseillaise was not written in Marseille. In which city on the Rhine was it composed in 1792?
source_excerpt: It was written in 1792 by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle in Strasbourg after the First French Republic declared war against Austria.

extra.why_interesting: The name points firmly at Marseille, so the player's instinct is wrong; the song was actually written at the opposite end of France, near the German border.
extra.verification_notes: Rouget de Lisle composed La Marseillaise in Strasbourg in April 1792, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Marseillaise).

explanation: Army officer Rouget de Lisle wrote it overnight as a war song for the Rhine army, and it only got its name later when volunteers from Marseille sang it on their march to Paris.

question: True or false: Spain's national anthem has no official lyrics, so Spanish players stand silent while it plays before matches.
source_excerpt: It is one of only three national anthems in the world – along with those of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo – that have no official lyrics.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture footballers mouthing anthems before matches and assume every anthem has words; Spanish players stand silent because there is officially nothing to sing.
extra.verification_notes: The Marcha Real has no official lyrics (unchanged as of 2026), so players generally stand silent; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcha_Real

explanation: The Marcha Real is one of a handful of wordless anthems in the world, and several attempts to agree official lyrics have failed for political reasons.

question: Red, white and blue are so common that every national flag on Earth uses at least one of them, except one. Which Caribbean country's flag has none of those three colours?
source_excerpt: The flag of Jamaica ... a gold saltire, which divides the flag into four sections: two of them green (top and bottom) and two black (hoist and fly).

extra.why_interesting: Red, white and blue feel like just three of many flag colours, yet every single national flag uses at least one of them except for one, and the player has to work out which.
extra.verification_notes: Jamaica's flag (green, gold, black) is the only national flag without red, white or blue, and Mauritania ceased to be an exception after adding red in 2017; I found no newer change.

explanation: Jamaica's flag uses only black, green and gold, and it became the sole exception in 2017 when Mauritania added red bands to its previously green-and-gold flag.
